newsitem.title: NORWAY: Rags-to-riches career for Norway entrepreneur.
newsitem.headline: Rags-to-riches career for Norway entrepreneur.

text.p: Written off as a no-hoper at school, Kjell Inge Roekke has proven his teachers very wrong, displaying enough charisma and drive to emerge as one of Norway's most successful entrepreneurs.

Roekke, 38, heads Resource Group International (RGI) and will soon take the biggest single stake in one of the largest industrial groups in Scandanavia with the merger of RGI and offshore group Aker ASA.
The new group announced on Tuesday -- Aker RGI ASA -- will have annual revenues of 19 billion crowns ($2.93 billion) and a market captialisation of nine billion crowns.
In just nine months Roekke and business partner Bjoern Rune Gjelsted have manoeuvered corporate upstart RGI to a fusion with Aker, one of Norway's oldest established companies.
Not bad considering RGI was only launched on the Oslo Bourse in July. It has already become one of the country's largest investment groups.

A self-made millionaire, Roekke began his career without a penny at 17 on a fish factory trawler in the Arctic. Today RGI's seafood business is the world's largest white fish fishing and processing operation.
An almost daily fixture in the Norwegian media, bespectacled Roekke cuts a suave figure among Oslo's business set with his reputation for fast boats and penchant for elegant women.
But his fast-track image belies fierce ambition.
"I've tied up almost my entire fortune in RGI and Aker, so I'm personally dependent on Aker RGI proving a success," Roekke said in a statement announcing the proposed merger.
But he rejected speculation of his desire to lead the new company, which will be one of the largest industrial concerns in Scandinavia.
"I've no vanity about positions. My sole concern is to ensure that the best people lead the group at all times."
Born in the tiny town of Molde on Norway's northwest coast, Roekke was told by a teacher as a young teenager that success for him would mean passing his driving test.
The unruly pupil was thrown out before finishing school, a just end to his education, Roekke agreed, when he recently turned up for a school reunion -- in his private jet.

With his quick mind and athletic build, he often won local cross-country ski competitions, despite being smaller than most of his peers. It was during one such competition that he met his close friend and later business partner Gjelsten.

Gjelsten has taken the lead role in RGI's activities with Aker, becoming chairman in the board after RGI bought a 30 percent stake earlier this year. He will also chair the board of the new merged company.
Apart from fishing, RGI's interests include sports goods and outdoor apparel, shipbuilding, real estate, packaging office supplies and finance.
Registered in the Netherlands Antilles, RGI is headquartered in Oslo. Roekke has another home in Seattle on the U.S. westcoast.
But the Molde boy often returns to his home town, drawn back by his mother's meatballs and Molde's soccer club, which, of course, he owns. ($1=6.496 Norwegian Crown)
